think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 48-year-old asymptomatic female nonsmoker presenting with an incidental 2.5 cm solitary subpleural pulmonary nodule characterized by irregular, partly spiculate margins, peripheral ground-glass halo, pleural tags, and pleural thickening. The presentation strongly mimics primary bronchogenic carcinoma (lung adenocarcinoma) or solitary tuberculoma. Peripheral eosinophil count and routine laboratories were completely normal, masking an underlying parasitic etiology.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission workup encompasses the initial routine chest radiograph, physical examination, normal laboratory workup including serum eosinophils, thoracic CT scan detailing the morphology of the right lower lobe subpleural nodule, pulmonary function testing, and non-diagnostic bronchoscopy. The breakpoint occurs just prior to surgical intervention (wedge resection) and histopathological examination.
3. Differential Distinctions: Bronchogenic carcinoma is the primary clinical suspicion given the spiculate, solid subpleural nodule with pleural retraction in a middle-aged adult, but histopathology reveals inflammatory organizing pneumonia with trematode ova rather than malignancy. Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP) typically causes bilateral fluctuating consolidations and symptoms, whereas here it was a focal solitary pseudotumor. Pulmonary tuberculosis can present as an asymptomatic solitary nodule (tuberculoma), but pathognomonic operculated trematode ova identify Paragonimus westermani.
case_prompt:
A 48-year-old woman is evaluated after an incidental right lung base nodule is detected on a routine screening chest radiograph. She is entirely asymptomatic and specifically denies chest pain, cough, dyspnea, or hemoptysis. She has no history of tobacco smoking, pneumothorax, or pleural effusion.

On physical examination, vital signs are normal and examination of the chest and other systems is unremarkable.

Baseline laboratory testing, including a complete blood count and serum eosinophil count, is normal.

A computed tomography (CT) scan of the thorax confirms the presence of a solitary 2.5 cm solid subpleural nodule in the posterior basal segment of the right lower lobe. The nodule exhibits irregular, partly spiculate margins with focal peripheral ground-glass opacity, partly broad pleural attachment, several pleural tags, and adjacent pleural and extrapleural fat thickening. The lesion has slightly heterogeneous low attenuation without calcification and demonstrates no significant contrast enhancement. Surrounding panlobular emphysema is present. There is no hilar or mediastinal lymphadenopathy, pleural effusion, or pneumothorax, and no other lung lesions are identified. Pulmonary function testing and bronchoscopy are normal.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered as the foremost concern given the solitary 2.5 cm subpleural nodule with irregular spiculate borders, pleural tags, and peripheral ground-glass halo in a 48-year-old patient; however, surgical resection demonstrated a parasitic inflammatory organizing pneumonia and coexistent aspergilloma rather than neoplastic disease.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The lesion was irregular 2.5 cm solid subpleural nodule with focal peripheral ground-glass opacity and partly spiculate margin. The lesion had partly broad pleural attachment and several pleural tags with adjacent pleural thickening and extrapleural fat thickening.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to subpleural consolidation and ground-glass attenuation, but peripheral blood counts and serum eosinophils were completely normal, and histology identified a distinct infectious etiology rather than idiopathic organizing pneumonia.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Physical examination and blood tests including serum eosinophil count were normal.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Histopathologic examination of the resected subpleural nodule demonstrated organizing pneumonia with bronchioles filled with necrotic debris and degenerated parasitic ova morphologically diagnostic of the lung fluke Paragonimus westermani, alongside a focal 2 mm aspergilloma.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: On histopathology, peripheral organizing pneumonia by paragonimiasis and coexistent small subpleural aspergilloma was noted (Figure 4)... These scattered degenerated parasitic eggs were morphologically consistent with ova of Paragonimus westermani.

editor_comments: Standardized admission diagnostic case for pulmonary paragonimiasis (Foodborne Trematodes) presenting as an incidental solitary pulmonary nodule mimicking lung cancer. Admission breakpoint established prior to surgical wedge resection.
